parts:
Dear ggplot2 group,

Firstly, i would like to wish to everybody  Merry Christmas and a happy new year !!  My name is Efstathios-Iason Vlachavas, I'm from Greece and I'm currently working as a PhD candidate at National Hellenic Research Foundation under the team of Metabolic Engineering & Bioinformatics, in Greece (http://www.eie.gr/nhrf/institutes/ibrb/programmes/metabolicengineering-en.html). I'm using R/Bioconductor about one year, but i recently discovered and have a first look in ggplot2 capabilities and documentation !! In detail, because im my current project im dealing mainly with microarray technology, & besides my main analysis, i'm also trying to build some pipelines regarding exploratory data analysis. Thus, i want to produce more elegant and higher quality graphics and plots regarding both my project analysis and for my pipelines--so,

As i have searched in the updated ggplot2 cheatsheet, 
http://www.rstudio.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/ggplot2-cheatsheet-2.0.pdf,

and also in other pipelines(i.e. RNA-seq analysis from Bioconductor http://www.bioconductor.org/help/workflows/rnaseqGene/), 

i have mainly experienced problems about creating some specific plots of interest:

In detail, a first "naive" function i created, was to deal with the output of function topTable from limma, and create a volcano plot, like below:

volcano.r <- function(object, FC_cutoff_1, FC_cutoff_2, pval_cutoff) { # where object is the output of topTable
  
  results <- object
  results$threshold <- "1"
  a <- subset(results, adj.P.Val < pval_cutoff & logFC > FC_cutoff_1)
  results[rownames(a), "threshold"] <- "2"
  b <- subset(results, adj.P.Val < pval_cutoff & logFC < FC_cutoff_2 )
  results[rownames(b), "threshold"] <- "3"
  
  volcano <- ggplot(data=results, aes(x=logFC, y=-1*log10(adj.P.Val), colour=threshold,      label=SYMBOL))
  
  volcano <- volcano + geom_point() + scale_color_manual(values=c("black","red","green"),   labels=c("Not Significant", "Upregulated", "Downregulated"), name="key/Legend") 
  
  volcano2 <- volcano + theme(legend.text=element_text(size=16))
  print(volcano2)
  ggsave(filename="eleos.jpeg", plot=volcano2)

}
(im posting the code in order to illustrate my main question below)


In this specific case, here i can distinguish the aesthetics regarding the data frame, both for the x and the y axis. However, my main difficulty was to try to create some general boxplots, histograms and Q-Q plots regarding for instance a specific microarray dataset in R, as in this case i don't deal with data frames, but mainly with ExpressionSets or matrices. Thus, i could not understand how to appropriately define the aesthetics, because here all the rows are the genes, and the columns represent the different samples. So,

1) Is there a tutorial or book regarding high-throughput data analysis with ggplot2, especially with examples for microarray data ?

2) Or is it possible to provide me with a small idea or a brief explanation on this matter, or where i could look to deal with my issue, as my main goal is to learn how to create these specific plots for microarray expression sets(boxplots, histograms and quantile-quantile plots) ??


Thank you in advance for your time and patience, and i hope i don't disturb anyone with any naive questions--but any suggestions or help on this matter would be beneficial for a newby like me !!

Best Regards,

Efstathios

Efstathios, 

It's been a while, but I have done some exploratory visualizations of microarray and RNAseq data using ggplot2. To answer your questions:

1) to my knowledge such a thing does not exist, but there might be some things out there in personal scripts and gists.
2) It sounds like you just need to transpose your array. If you have a matrix as you describe just wrap it in as.data.frame(t("matrix goes here")). My understanding is that you'll want some sort of normalization of your matrix before plotting. 

If you have more specific questions related to plotting, could you dput() a subset of your dataset and provide a better description of what you want?

B

volcano.r <- function(object, FC_cutoff_1, FC_cutoff_2, pval_cutoff) { # where object is the output of topTable
  
  results <- object
  results$threshold <- "1"
  a <- subset(results, adj.P.Val < pval_cutoff & logFC > FC_cutoff_1)
  results[rownames(a), "threshold"] <- "2"
  b <- subset(results, adj.P.Val < pval_cutoff & logFC < FC_cutoff_2 )
  results[rownames(b), "threshold"] <- "3"
  
  volcano <- ggplot(data=results, aes(x=logFC, y=-1*log10(adj.P.Val), colour=threshold,      label=SYMBOL))
  
  volcano <- volcano + geom_point() + scale_color_manual(values=c("black","red","green"),   labels=c("Not Significant", "Upregulated", "Downregulated"), name="key/Legend")

  print(volcano2)
  ggsave(filename="eleos.jpeg", plot=volcano2)

Thank you in advance for your time and patience, and i hope i don't disturb anyone with any naive questions--but any suggestions or help on this matter would be beneficial for a newby like me !!

Best Regards,

Efstathios

Hi Efstathios,

You don't have to use the tidyr package, but you do need to reshape
the data before plotting. You could do that with stats::reshape, with
reshape2::melt, data.table::melt, or tidyr::gather or any other means
you prefer. For details on the arguments to tidyr::gather see ?gather.

Histograms will need somewhat different treatment, perhaps

ggplot(x, aes(x = intensity, fill = Condition)) + geom_histogram() +
facet_wrap(~sample)

Best,
Ista

Yes, Ista's approach is better than what I was coming up with for summarizing across all samples. 

My approach was to extract the phenotype and matrix from the expressionSet object, transpose it, filter it for each gene and then plot it.  
https://gist.github.com/bhive01/aa15ac57546bc64b2f08

Then I ran into a plotting issue. 
Worked with mtcars. I don't get it. 

Anyway, this is helpful for checking the overall signal differences between samples, but I think what you're after is a comparison of differences between Normal and Diseased for each gene, but this would be impossible to read and take ages to plot. You need to filter your dataset for things that are different by some statistical test (maybe an output of the affy analysis) and then plot those that have interesting differences. I never had enough samples to really differentiate treatments, but if you have 30 and 30 you should be able to easily test for differences.

Yes, Ista's approach is better than what I was coming up with for summarizing across all samples. 

My approach was to extract the phenotype and matrix from the expressionSet object, transpose it, filter it for each gene and then plot it.  
https://gist.github.com/bhive01/aa15ac57546bc64b2f08

Then I ran into a plotting issue. 
Worked with mtcars. I don't get it. 

Anyway, this is helpful for checking the overall signal differences between samples, but I think what you're after is a comparison of differences between Normal and Diseased for each gene, but this would be impossible to read and take ages to plot. You need to filter your dataset for things that are different by some statistical test (maybe an output of the affy analysis) and then plot those that have interesting differences. I never had enough samples to really differentiate treatments, but if you have 30 and 30 you should be able to easily test for differences.

Dear Ista,
